b: Marriage is indeed complex, and it takes much in the way of humility to survive the years. Is luck involved? Perhaps, but I tend to think it is more blessings from what was gleaned in one’s own family of origin. On the topic of co-habitation, the percentage of young people choosing this is off the charts - like 70-80%. My wife and I have done marriage enrichment for over 20 years. It is rare for both the man and the woman to list separate addresses. Why is this an issue? At its core level, co-habitation is more of a trial of “will this work out?”and lacking in commitment. It often follows the thought that “I will stay with you, honey, as long as you make me feel good and happy.” An attorney who worked with us on these projects taught that the divorce rate for co-habitation couples is a full 50% higher than the typical oft-quoted national rate of 50%. That would be 75% (half of 50% plus 50% = 75%). That almost mirrors, or is in fact somewhat low, for the rate of co-habiting couples. A coincidence? I don’t think so. The other strand of truth here for these couples is the frequent desire of avoidance of children. Yes, children cost money and sleep and many things - but they mostly glue couples to one another unlike any other aspect of a relationship. Certainly, couples with children do split, but they are much less likely to do so because of a young one who depends deeply on the love and support of both parents. Marriage provides the backbone of this commitment, which benefits society in countless ways. Co-habitation is much more easily walked away from than legal marriage, with much less protection for the parties, depending on state laws for common law arrangements.
